\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

LLM-based automated program repair systems increasingly rely on test-time compute scaling: generating $K$ candidate patches and selecting the best via a verifier~\cite{snell2024scaling}. Full execution verification is reliable but expensive (\$1--3 per candidate at repository scale\footnote{Based on per-instance costs reported by \citet{yang2024sweagent} and \citet{xia2024agentless}.}), driving demand for execution-free alternatives. Three distinct formulations have emerged for this task: \textbf{generation-based simulation}~\cite{meta2025cwm,maimon2026selfexecution} predicts execution output strings per test; \textbf{trajectory-level scoring}~\cite{shum2025swerm} predicts a binary patch verdict without per-test decomposition; and \textbf{per-test classification}~\cite{ni2023lever,chen2023codet} predicts a pass/fail token per test. Each makes different tradeoffs between diagnostic granularity, output complexity, and inference cost.

Despite active development along each axis, no prior work provides a controlled comparison holding model capacity, training data, and compute constant. Practitioners choosing a formulation for their verification pipeline must rely on results from different models, different datasets, and different evaluation protocols. Whether one formulation is uniformly preferable, or whether the choice depends on properties of the code being verified, remains an open empirical question.

We present the first systematic comparison of these three formulations across two model families (Qwen3, DeepSeek-Coder), two complexity levels (function-level and repository-level), and multiple seeds. Our central finding is that \emph{formulation effectiveness is complexity-dependent and model-contingent}: at function-level complexity, all three formulations achieve statistically equivalent accuracy regardless of model family; at repository-level complexity, formulations diverge sharply, with the magnitude and direction of divergence depending on model and tokenizer properties rather than formulation design alone. Figure~\ref{fig:reformulation} illustrates the three formulations.

We make the following contributions:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Formulation equivalence at low complexity.} On function-level benchmarks, \cls{}, \cwm{}, and \traj{} achieve near-identical accuracy across two model families (Qwen3-4B: 88.4/87.2/86.3\%, 5 seeds; DeepSeek-6.7B: 86.9/86.8\%, 2 seeds). The \cls{}--\cwm{} gap is 0.02--1.24\pp{}, within seed noise in both cases. This null result establishes that classification is not inherently easier than generation when execution outputs are short and structured.

\item \textbf{Complexity-dependent divergence.} At repository-level complexity with Qwen3, \cls{} achieves 19--26\pp{} higher accuracy than \cwm{} (4B: 25.59\pp{}; 8B: 19.31\pp{}), driven by format compliance collapse: 54--74\% of \cwm{} outputs are unparseable, and parseable-only accuracy degrades from 42.9\% (4B) to 38.5\% (8B). Whether this divergence generalizes across model families or is tokenizer/model-specific is under investigation (DeepSeek repo-level results pending). Both outcomes are informative: consistency would confirm complexity as the primary moderator; divergence would identify model properties as a critical design variable.

\item \textbf{Error complementarity and ensemble potential.} \cls{} and \cwm{} exhibit systematically opposite error patterns at function level: \cls{} over-predicts passing (75.5\% of errors are false negatives) while \cwm{} over-predicts failure (83.1\% false positives). An oracle ensemble achieves 90.63\% (+3.12\pp{} over the best single formulation), suggesting that the formulations capture complementary aspects of code behavior.

\item \textbf{Diagnostic granularity at equivalent accuracy.} Per-test classification achieves statistically equivalent variant-level accuracy to trajectory-level scoring (TOST equivalence $p = 0.007$, $\pm$2\pp{} margin) while providing per-test diagnostic signals at 217$\times$ higher throughput than generation (1 output token vs.\ avg 477). This enables failure localization without accuracy or efficiency cost relative to coarser formulations.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Execution Simulation for Code.}
Code World Models~\cite{meta2025cwm} mid-train a 32B LLM on execution traces to predict output strings, establishing the generation-based paradigm for execution-free verification.
Self-Execution~\cite{maimon2026selfexecution} extends this with step-by-step trace prediction.
CodeMind~\cite{liu2024codemind} evaluates code reasoning along multiple dimensions including execution prediction.
SolidCoder~\cite{lee2026solidcoder} bridges mental simulation and actual execution via concrete feedback.
Abdollahi et al.~\cite{abdollahi2025demystifying} identify systematic failure modes in LLM trace prediction, including position-dependent errors.
All share a generation formulation whose cost scales with output length. We provide the first controlled comparison of this formulation against classification and trajectory-level alternatives at matched model capacity, revealing that generation reliability is contingent on both code complexity and model/tokenizer properties.

\paragraph{LLM-based Verification for Code Repair.}
SWE-RM~\cite{shum2025swerm} trains a trajectory-level reward model for patch ranking without execution.
Patch Reasoner~\cite{xu2025patchreasoner} uses chain-of-thought reasoning for patch verification.
Snell et al.~\cite{snell2024scaling} show that test-time scaling via verification outperforms parameter scaling.
S*~\cite{li2025sstar} combines execution-grounded selection with model-based scoring.
VG-Search~\cite{chen2025vgsearch} finds that finer-grained verification improves selection efficiency.
These works treat verification granularity as a design choice but do not compare the underlying formulation (classification vs.\ generation) at controlled capacity. We provide this comparison, finding that the granularity choice interacts with complexity level.

\paragraph{Process vs.\ Outcome Supervision.}
Lightman et al.~\cite{lightman2023letsverify} demonstrate that process-based reward models (verifying each reasoning step) outperform outcome-based models (verifying only the final answer) for mathematical reasoning.
Uesato et al.~\cite{uesato2022solving} show similar advantages for process feedback in math word problems.
Our per-test classification is structurally analogous to process supervision: each test verdict corresponds to an intermediate verification step, while trajectory-level scoring corresponds to outcome supervision. Our finding that per-test and trajectory-level achieve equivalent accuracy (TOST $p = 0.007$) with per-test providing additional diagnostic value parallels the process supervision literature, where step-level verification enables error localization at no accuracy cost.

\paragraph{Verification-in-the-Loop Repair.}
CodeRL~\cite{le2022coderl} trains a critic model to provide execution feedback for RL-based code generation.
AlphaCode~\cite{li2022alphacode} uses massive sampling with test-based filtering for competition programming.
Reflexion~\cite{shinn2023reflexion} uses verbal self-reflection on execution results to iteratively improve agent performance.
These systems demonstrate that verification quality is a primary bottleneck for iterative repair. Our comparison of verification formulations is complementary: the efficiency and diagnostic granularity of the verifier directly affects the viability of verification-in-the-loop approaches at scale.

\paragraph{Learned Code Verifiers.}
LEVER~\cite{ni2023lever} trains a classifier to re-rank code candidates by predicting execution correctness.
CodeT~\cite{chen2023codet} uses dual execution agreement as a verification signal.
Both target execution-free deployment via classification-style training. Unlike candidate-level ranking, we provide per-test diagnostic verdicts and compare classification against generation on the same model, data, and compute budget, isolating the effect of task formulation.

\paragraph{Automated Program Repair.}
SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} and SWE-bench Verified~\cite{chowdhury2024swebenchverified} provide standard benchmarks for repository-level repair.
SWE-agent~\cite{yang2024sweagent} uses tool-augmented agents; Agentless~\cite{xia2024agentless} demonstrates a simpler pipeline.
Yang et al.~\cite{yang2025aprsurvey} survey LLM-based repair, identifying verification as a persistent bottleneck.
These systems rely on execution-based validation, with cost scaling linearly in candidates. Per-test verification provides failure-localized signals that could support targeted re-repair.

\paragraph{Predictive Mutation Testing.}
Predicting test outcomes for code mutations without execution has been studied in software engineering~\cite{tufano2019predictive,kim2022predictive}. Our per-test classification formulation shares this problem structure: given a code change (mutation/patch) and a test, predict pass or fail. We extend this line to LLM-based verification at repository scale, comparing it against alternative formulations (generation, trajectory-level) for the first time.

\paragraph{Classification vs.\ Generation in NLP.}
Task framing affects model performance broadly: T5~\cite{raffel2020t5} and BART~\cite{lewis2020bart} demonstrate generation-classification tradeoffs under controlled capacity, while SQuAD~\cite{rajpurkar2016squad} shows that constraining output space can simplify tasks without sacrificing quality. We extend this lens to code verification, finding that code complexity moderates the tradeoff in a model-contingent manner.

## Abstract (v47)

\begin{abstract}
Execution-free verification for LLM-based code repair can be formulated in multiple ways, yet no controlled comparison exists across formulations at matched model capacity. We systematically evaluate three formulations: per-test binary classification (\cls{}), execution output generation (\cwm{}), and trajectory-level patch scoring, training on identical data with controlled model sizes (4B, 8B).

At function level, the three formulations achieve near-equivalent accuracy (\cls{} 88.43\% vs.\ \cwm{} 87.19\% at 4B, 5 seeds; TOST equivalence with trajectory-level at $p{=}0.007$). At repository level, formulation divergence amplifies to 19--26\pp{} (4B: 25.59\pp{}; 8B: 19.31\pp{}), with \cwm{} falling below majority baseline. However, this divergence is partially model-contingent: \cwm{} failures on Qwen3 concentrate in format non-compliance (unparseable rate 53.7\%$\to$73.8\% from 4B to 8B) rather than semantic prediction errors, and generation quality uniformly degrades with scale (parseable-only accuracy 42.9\%$\to$38.5\%). Whether this reflects a fundamental generation bottleneck or model-specific behavior remains open pending cross-model validation.

Two findings generalize across conditions. First, per-test classification provides diagnostic granularity (which specific tests fail) at equivalent trajectory-level accuracy, with the advantage concentrating in instances with $\geq$2 failing tests (31\% of instances, 55\% of oracle advantage). Second, formulations exhibit complementary error patterns: an oracle ensemble reaches 90.63\%, motivating complexity-aware routing rather than a single universal formulation.
\end{abstract}

## Introduction (v42)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

LLM-based automated program repair systems increasingly rely on test-time compute scaling: generating $K$ candidate patches and selecting the best via a verifier~\cite{snell2024scaling}. Full execution verification is reliable but expensive (\$1--3 per candidate at repository scale), driving demand for execution-free alternatives. Three distinct formulations have emerged for this task: \textbf{generation-based simulation}~\cite{meta2025cwm,maimon2026selfexecution} predicts execution output strings per test; \textbf{trajectory-level scoring}~\cite{shum2025swerm} predicts a binary patch verdict without per-test decomposition; and \textbf{per-test classification}~\cite{ni2023lever,chen2023codet} predicts a pass/fail token per test. Each makes different tradeoffs between diagnostic granularity, output complexity, and inference cost.

Despite active development along each axis, no prior work provides a controlled comparison holding model capacity, training data, and compute constant. Practitioners choosing a formulation for their verification pipeline must rely on results from different models, different datasets, and different evaluation protocols. Whether one formulation is uniformly preferable, or whether the choice depends on properties of the code being verified, remains an open empirical question.

We present the first systematic comparison of these three formulations across two model families (Qwen3, DeepSeek-Coder), two complexity levels (function-level and repository-level), and multiple seeds. Our central finding is that \emph{formulation effectiveness is complexity-dependent and model-contingent}: at function-level complexity, all three formulations achieve statistically equivalent accuracy regardless of model family; at repository-level complexity, formulations diverge sharply, with the magnitude and direction of divergence depending on model and tokenizer properties rather than formulation design alone.

Contributions:
1. Formulation equivalence at low complexity (gap 0.02--1.24pp)
2. Complexity-dependent divergence (19--26pp at repo level, model-contingent)
3. Error complementarity (oracle 90.63%)
4. Diagnostic granularity at equivalent accuracy (TOST p=0.007, 217× throughput)

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented the first controlled comparison of three formulations for execution-free code repair verification: per-test binary classification (\cls{}), execution output generation (\cwm{}), and trajectory-level scoring. Our central finding is that no single formulation dominates across all conditions; formulation effectiveness is complexity-dependent and, at repository scale, model-contingent.

At function level, \cls{} and \cwm{} achieve near-equivalent accuracy (gap 1.24\pp{} at 4B, TOST equivalence $p{=}0.007$), suggesting that the formulation choice matters less than model capacity and training data at this complexity tier. Whether this reflects a fundamental generation bottleneck or a model-specific tokenizer interaction remains an open empirical question pending cross-model validation.

Two formulation-level properties generalize independent of model choice. First, per-test classification provides diagnostic granularity at equivalent trajectory-level accuracy, identifying which specific tests a patch fails. This advantage concentrates in instances with $\geq$2 fail-to-pass tests (31\% of instances, contributing 55\% of total oracle advantage). Second, the 1-token classification formulation yields a 217$\times$ throughput advantage over variable-length generation, an inherent property of the output-length asymmetry.

Error complementarity between formulations (oracle ensemble: 90.63\%) suggests that the practitioner's choice need not be exclusive. Classification and generation exhibit complementary failure patterns, motivating routing strategies that select formulations based on predicted instance complexity.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Execution Simulation for Code.}
Code World Models~\cite{meta2025cwm} mid-train a 32B LLM on execution traces to predict output strings, establishing the generation-based paradigm for execution-free verification.
Self-Execution~\cite{maimon2026selfexecution} extends this with step-by-step trace prediction.
CodeMind~\cite{liu2024codemind} evaluates code reasoning along multiple dimensions including execution prediction.
SolidCoder~\cite{lee2026solidcoder} bridges mental simulation and actual execution via concrete feedback.
Abdollahi et al.~\cite{abdollahi2025demystifying} identify systematic failure modes in LLM trace prediction, including position-dependent errors.
All share a generation formulation whose cost scales with output length. We provide the first controlled comparison of this formulation against classification and trajectory-level alternatives at matched model capacity, revealing that generation reliability is contingent on both code complexity and model/tokenizer properties.

\paragraph{LLM-based Verification for Code Repair.}
SWE-RM~\cite{shum2025swerm} trains a trajectory-level reward model for patch ranking without execution.
Patch Reasoner~\cite{xu2025patchreasoner} uses chain-of-thought reasoning for patch verification.
Snell et al.~\cite{snell2024scaling} show that test-time scaling via verification outperforms parameter scaling.
S*~\cite{li2025sstar} combines execution-grounded selection with model-based scoring.
VG-Search~\cite{chen2025vgsearch} finds that finer-grained verification improves selection efficiency.
These works treat verification granularity as a design choice but do not compare the underlying formulation (classification vs.\ generation) at controlled capacity. We provide this comparison, finding that the granularity choice interacts with complexity level.

\paragraph{Process vs.\ Outcome Supervision.}
Lightman et al.~\cite{lightman2023letsverify} demonstrate that process-based reward models (verifying each reasoning step) outperform outcome-based models (verifying only the final answer) for mathematical reasoning.
Uesato et al.~\cite{uesato2022solving} show similar advantages for process feedback in math word problems.
Our per-test classification is structurally analogous to process supervision: each test verdict corresponds to an intermediate verification step, while trajectory-level scoring corresponds to outcome supervision. CodeRL~\cite{le2022coderl} trains a critic model to provide execution feedback for RL-based code generation.

LEVER~\cite{ni2023lever} trains a classifier to re-rank code candidates by predicting execution correctness.

Predicting test outcomes for code mutations without execution has been studied in software engineering~\cite{tufano2019predictive,kim2022predictive}. Our per-test classification formulation shares this problem structure: given a code change (mutation/patch) and a test, predict pass or fail. We extend this line to LLM-based verification at repository scale, comparing it against alternative formulations (generation, trajectory-level) for the first time.
